post.description: Find ISRCTN studies on a topic, from a sponsor or funder, in a country or with a recruitment status, before calling study for the full record. For a known ISRCTN, URL or NCT/EudraCT/IRAS number, call study directly.

condition.description: Condition or disease, matched as a phrase, e.g. "breast cancer".

country.description: Recruitment country as the registry names it ("United Kingdom", "United States of America", "Korea, South"); UK, US, USA and common aliases work. "United Kingdom" also matches studies that list only England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.

funder.description: Funder name, matched as a phrase, e.g. "Wellcome Trust".

intervention.description: Intervention, drug or device, matched as a phrase, e.g. "tranexamic acid".

page_size.description:
Studies per page.

Provider reference: minimum 1; maximum 50; default 10.

page_token.description: next_page_token from the previous page; send the same filters again.

phase.description: Any of these phases; combined phases match both (PHASE2 matches Phase I/II, Phase II and Phase II/III).

registered_from.description: Registered (ISRCTN assigned) on or after this date, YYYY-MM-DD. Pattern: ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$.

registered_to.description: Registered on or before this date, YYYY-MM-DD. Pattern: ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$.

sponsor.description: Sponsor organisation, matched as a phrase, e.g. "University of Oxford".

status.description: Keep studies whose overall or recruitment status is any of these, computed as ISRCTN computes them (see overall_status and recruitment_status). The registry does not index computed statuses, so each page is filtered after fetching: total_count is null and a page can come back short with a next_page_token.

study_type.description:
Primary study design.

Provider reference: allowed values ["INTERVENTIONAL", "OBSERVATIONAL"].

term.description: Free text searched across the whole record, with AND, OR, NOT, quoted phrases and parentheses, e.g. "tranexamic acid" AND trauma. Field constraints from the ISRCTN API also work (condition:asthma). Unbalanced quotes or parentheses are refused: the registry would silently match nothing.

title.description: Words in the public or scientific title, or the acronym, matched as a phrase, e.g. "RECOVERY".

updated_since.description: Record edited on or after this date, YYYY-MM-DD. Pattern: ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$.

200.description:
Search the ISRCTN registry (GET /api/query). Combine free text with condition, intervention, sponsor, funder, title, recruitment country, phase, study type, registration or update dates, and a status filter computed the way ISRCTN computes recruitment status. Returns one page of study summaries, newest registration first, each with its ISRCTN, DOI, statuses, phases, conditions, lead sponsor, enrolment, key dates, countries and any ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, plus a page token. An empty result is a valid empty page.

The response contains the tool result directly.

The provider identifies `studies` as the primary payload key.

| --- | --- | --- |
| `acronym` | string |  |
| `brief_title` | string | Public title. |
| `completion_date` | string | Overall study end date. |

| `enrollment` | object | Final enrolment (ACTUAL) when reported, else the target (ESTIMATED). |
| `has_results` | boolean | Whether the record reports results: a results article, basic or plain-English results, or interim results. |
| `interventions` | object[] |  |
| `isrctn` | string | The study's ISRCTN, e.g. ISRCTN86750102. |
| `last_updated_date` | string | Date the record was last edited. |
| `lead_sponsor` | object | The first sponsor the record lists. |
| `nct_ids` | string[] | ClinicalTrials.gov numbers the study lists; pass one to the clinicaltrials-gov provider's study function. |
| `official_title` | string | Scientific title. |
| `overall_status` | string | Overall study status as ISRCTN computes it: an editorial override (STOPPED, SUSPENDED, ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION) wins, otherwise ONGOING until the overall end date and COMPLETED after it. null when the record has neither. |

value.brief_title: CRASH2 Trial, a large randomised placebo-controlled trial among trauma patients with significant haemorrhage of the effects of an antifibrinolytic treatment on death and transfusion requirement
value.citation: Roberts, I (2004): CRASH2 Trial, a large randomised placebo-controlled trial among trauma patients with significant haemorrhage of the effects of an antifibrinolytic treatment on death and transfusion requirement. ISRCTN. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN86750102

eligibility.exclusion_criteria: The fundamental eligibility criterion is the responsible doctor's 'uncertainty' as to whether or not to use an antifibrinolytic agent in a particular adult with traumatic haemorrhage. Patients for whom the responsible doctor considers there is a clear indication for antifibrinolytic therapy should not be randomised. Likewise, patients for whom there is considered to be a clear contraindication to antifibrinolytic therapy (such as, perhaps, those who have clinical evidence of a thrombotic disseminated intravascular coagulation) should not be randomised. Where the responsible doctor is substantially uncertain as to whether or not to use an antifibrinolytic, all these patients are eligible for randomisation and should be considered for the trial. There are no other pre-specified exclusion criteria.
eligibility.inclusion_criteria: All adult trauma patients who are considered to be at risk of significant haemorrhage and are within 8 hours of the injury, are eligible for trial entry if they appear to be at least 16 years old. There are no other pre-specified exclusion criteria, as the fundamental eligibility criterion is the responsible doctor's 'uncertainty' whether or not to use tranexamic acid (TXA) in a particular adult with traumatic haemorrhage. Patients for whom there is considered by the responsible doctor to be a clear indication for TXA should not be randomised. Likewise, any for whom there is considered to be a clear contraindication to TXA (such as, perhaps, those who have clinical evidence of a thrombotic disseminated intravascular coagulation) should not be randomised. All those for whom the responsible doctor is substantially uncertain as to whether or not to use an anti-fibrinolytic agent are eligible for randomisation, and as many such patients as possible should be considered for the trial.

value.objectives:
Because the coagulation abnormalities that occur after injury are similar to those after surgery, it is possible that antifibrinolytic agents might also reduce blood loss, the need for transfusion and mortality following trauma. However, to date there has been only one small randomised controlled trial (70 randomised patients, drug versus placebo: 0 versus 3 deaths) of the effect of antifibrinolytic agents in major trauma. As a result, there is insufficient evidence to either support or refute a clinically important treatment effect. Systemic antifibrinolytic agents have been used in the management of eye injuries where there is some evidence that they reduce the rate of secondary haemorrhage. 

CRASH2 aims to determine the effect of the early administration of the antifibrinolytic agent tranexamic acid (TXA) on death and transfusion requirement in adult trauma patients with ongoing significant haemorrhage, or who are considered to be at risk of significant haemorrhage. In addition, the effect on the risk of non-fatal vascular events (either haemorrhagic or occlusive) will be assessed. 

The initial stages of the trial was funded by the London School of Hygiene, the Bupa Foundation and the Moulton Charitable Trust. In 2007, this trial obtained main funding from the NIHR Health Technology Assessment Programme, which will fund this trial from April 2007 to September 2010. 

More information on the CRASH2 trial can be found at: http://www.nets.nihr.ac.uk/projects/hta/0630320 

As of 16/06/2008, the CRASH2 trial will conduct sub-group analyses "CRASH-2 Intracranial Bleeding Study (IBS)" (start date: October 2009) to study the effect of TXA in participants who also have traumatic brain injury (TBI). About 40% of participants out of 9,000 enrolled so far have TBI. Details of this sub-study can be found at: http://www.nets.nihr.ac.uk/projects/hta/0910201 

Hypothesis: Early administration of TXA can prevent the occurrence or increase of intracranial bleeding in patients with TBI and significant bleeding. 

On 21/08/2009 the anticipated start and end dates of this trial were changed from 01/05/2005 and 30/04/2010 to 01/04/2007 and 30/09/2010, respectively. 

This trial completed follow-up on the 02/03/2010, and the record was updated to reflect this on 09/07/2010.

primary_outcomes.measure:
The primary outcome measure is death in hospital within 4 weeks of injury (causes of death will be classified).

An additional outcome measure for the sub-group analyses (added as of 18/06/2008): 
1. Increase in volume of intracranial bleeding. A repeat CT scan will be carried out 24-48 hours after injury and compared to a clinical baseline CT scan.

secondary_outcomes.measure:
Secondary outcome measures will be receipt of a blood transfusion, volume of blood transfused, surgical intervention and the occurrence of vascular events (haemorrhagic stroke, occlusive stroke, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, clinically diagnosed deep vein thrombosis). Data will be recorded on a single sided outcome form which can be completed entirely from the hospital notes. There will be no additional tests.

Additional outcome measures for the sub-group analyses (added as of 18/06/2008): 
A repeat CT scan will be carried out 24 - 48 hours after injury and compared to a clinical baseline CT scan to assess the following:
1. Frequency of progressive haematomas
2. Frequency of delayed haematomas
3. New focal ischaemic lesions
